claims.text: The alloy has a distinct lamellar, multiphase eutectic microstructure with well-defined phase boundaries.
Differences in elemental composition between phases create local galvanic cells when protective oxide films are removed.
Mechanical wear removes protective oxide or passivation layers.
Removal of passivation exposes fresh metal at galvanically coupled phase interfaces.
Micro-galvanic coupling at exposed phase interfaces accelerates localized corrosion at phase boundaries.
Localized corrosion preferentially softens or degrades particular phases.
Corrosion-induced loss of hardness and integrity increases subsequent wear.
Wear-enhanced corrosion and corrosion-enhanced wear form a positive feedback loop.
The positive feedback loop produces accelerated overall degradation during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
The simultaneous test will produce higher total degradation than isolated wear or isolated corrosion baselines.
Wear volume during coupled exposure will exceed the wear response under isolated wear.
Corrosion rate during coupled exposure will exceed the corrosion response under isolated corrosion.
The proposed comparison uses isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and simultaneous wear-corrosion groups under matched temperature and duration conditions.
The proposed coupled exposure is conducted at 300°C in 0.5 M NaCl for six hours using reciprocating sliding.
The mechanism is expected to apply to clearly multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys near 300°C in chloride-containing environments.
Substantially lower temperatures or changes in alloy composition and processing may suppress the proposed synergy.
Quantitative acceleration factors depend on phase distribution, interfacial chemistry, and processing-induced heterogeneity.
The qualitative wear-corrosion feedback mechanism is well supported.
